chronicle: At the Marchward trestle, Rhinofire drew the shape of what lies north from two reluctant sources: a duelist's field account of a hand going black and a listening face, and an exile's admission that the upstream structure is a pre-Transition authentication site holding the Council's backup purification sequence — gone silent eight months ago, and perhaps listening still. One final question — what should I not let it hear? — found the edge of what Eredan will carry. He refused it, finally, and returned to his barley.

turns.player: Ask the hostel-keeper if anyone else has come through from the northeast trail recently — one more voice before you commit the direction.
turns.summary: The hostel-keeper describes a lone traveler from the Disputed Zone cutoff, asking after the north road; he left a sealed, unmarked note behind.
turns.narration:
The hostel-keeper is a broad woman with flour on her apron and the unhurried manner of someone who has heard every kind of question and stopped being surprised by any of them. She's wiping down the counter when you put the question to her — anyone through from the northeast trail lately, before the melt turned the ground soft?

She thinks for a moment, setting the cloth down. "Two, maybe three days back. A man alone, coming down from the Disputed Zone cutoff. Kept his hood up, which people do, so I didn't press. But he paid in valley coin and he asked about the road north — not the way to the Redline, the *other* north, the one that goes into the Zone proper." She picks the cloth back up. "He ate, he slept, he was gone before I came down in the morning. Left the bed neat, which I appreciated."

Marrow shifts on the rafter above the counter — you didn't see it get up there, but here it is, watching the keeper with the specific calm attention it reserves for things that are concluding. The keeper glances up at it, unsurprised in the way border-town people learn not to be surprised by anything, and goes back to wiping.

"He left something, actually. Forgot it or didn't want it." She reaches under the counter and sets down a small square of folded paper, sealed with a plain wax thumb-press. No mark, no name. "If you're going that direction anyway."

turns.player: Take the note and break the seal — read what was left.
turns.summary: Rhinofire breaks the seal on the unmarked note: a warning about the authentication site — it is waiting, not broken — and a single line about the wrong stag north of the second ford.
turns.narration:
The hostel-keeper slides the note across the counter without being asked — she's been waiting to be rid of it. The wax breaks clean under your thumb, plain, no sigil. Just a thumb.

Inside: six lines in a cramped, careful hand. The authentication site is not broken — it is waiting. Do not speak your name to it. Do not let it hear the water's composition — it will try to complete the protocol. If you are going anyway: the sequence it wants is the one the Council burned. It cannot be given. Tell it nothing and leave. The man who sent the survey crew back was not afraid. He was satisfied. Below that, a single line with no context: The wrong stag walks the treeline north of the second ford. Go around. No signature. The hand is educated — letters shaped with discipline — and the note smells faintly of something mineral, cold. Like stone after rain.

Marrow drops from the rafter onto the counter between you and the keeper, which she accepts with the equanimity of someone who has dealt with worse. The bird looks at the note. Then at you. Then at the treeline through the small east window, as if it already knows exactly which ford the second one is.

turns.player: Show the note to Eredan — he named the structure; he may recognize the hand or the warning's source.
turns.summary: Eredan reads the note without touching it, confirms the warning is accurate, and reveals that whoever wrote it has been north of the second ford — and recently.
turns.narration:
You cross the room and set the note on the table beside Eredan's bowl without a word. Just the paper, open, where he can read it.

He doesn't look up at first. Finishes chewing, puts his spoon down, then glances at it the way you'd glance at something you already know is going to cost you. His eyes move across the six lines slowly — too slowly for a man reading; the pace of someone making sure they haven't missed a word they hoped wasn't there.

When he's done he sits back. Doesn't touch the note.

"I don't know the hand," he says, and there's enough flatness in it that you believe him. "But the warning's right. Everything in it is right." He's quiet for a moment. "The wrong stag. That's not something people write down. That's something you only know if you've been north of the second ford." He looks up at you then — the first time he's met your eyes since his refusal. "Whoever wrote this has been there. Recently."

He pushes the note back toward you. Not away from him — toward you, specifically. His hands have stopped shaking for the first time since you sat down. "They're right about the sequence," he adds, quieter. "The Council burned it. There's no version of giving it to the structure that ends well. You go there, you say nothing. You let it run its authentication, it waits for what won't come, and eventually it stops waiting." A pause. "That's the theory. No one's stayed long enough to find out if it works."

chronicleCache.hash: d0|b|c|q|L1|To right the wrongs of the world
chronicleCache.text: You have become someone who carries a grievance older than your own name — a fury at wrongs not yet righted, a moral weight that sits in the chest like a coal still finding its heat. The Marchers know your face now, have registered your presence among them the way a wall registers a first crack: noted, not yet tested. The Ashwardens and the Unmakers have heard nothing particular about you, which means the world still holds its breath. Even the Stillhold watches from a wary distance, as if they sense something in you that hasn't declared itself yet. You have done nothing of consequence — not yet. That is the whole of the pressure.
